classification.difficultyReason: Foundation: directly apply the taught truncated-bar-baseline explanation to Faith's impression and the chart's exaggerated differences. Reading the close scores supports the same explanation without requiring a new strategy.

content.prompt: The average score of 5 classes on a maths test was graphed.

spec.description: Test scores. Score (%) vertical 71.7 to 73.0 by 0.1. Class A72.0, B72.9, C71.8, D71.9, E72.1. Equal-width bars, zero omitted. Graph sits right of parts a,b.
spec.answerVisibility: question; assessed misleading features intentionally retained

children.label: a
children.prompt: Faith says, “Class B’s average score was significantly higher than any other class.” Explain why Faith thinks this.

answer.short: Class B’s bar looks much taller because the vertical scale is truncated.
answer.worked: The graph starts at 71.7%, so B’s 72.9% bar appears much taller than the other bars.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Explain why this chart might be misleading.

answer.short: The 71.7% baseline exaggerates differences of at most 1.1 percentage points.
answer.worked: The highest score is 72.9% and the lowest is 71.8%, a difference of only 1.1 percentage points. Starting the bars at 71.7% makes this small difference look large.
